narrative:
The model predicted a 55% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your undergraduate GPA was the strongest influence. At 2.70 it sits well below the 3.23 average of students who were accepted, and this lower performance pulled the prediction strongly toward failure. Next, your third-year class ranking in decile 3 (compared with an average around 5.8 among accepted students) added further weight toward a likely bar exam failure. Finally, your upper-middle family income also nudged the outcome slightly higher, though this effect was smaller.

Taken together, these academic signals outweighed other details such as your LSAT score of 32.5 or your plan to attend full-time. The system therefore concluded you were more likely than not to struggle with the bar exam.

What you should do next is straightforward: strengthen your academic record. Retake challenging courses to raise your GPA, aim for a higher class rank, and consider retaking the LSAT. Once you can show clearer evidence of strong performance, reapply. Many students improve these exact areas and gain admission on a later attempt.
